blocks.en: "Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keeps the law, happy is he." — Proverbs 29:18 (NKJV / KJV tradition)
blocks.es_reference: "Sin visión, el pueblo perece; mas el que guarda la ley es bienaventurado." — Proverbios 29:18 (RVG)

blocks.en: Introduction — The Cupbearer Who Wept
blocks.es_reference: Introducción — El copero que lloró

blocks.en: The walls of Jerusalem lay in ruins. The gates were burned, the people were discouraged, and the enemies round about them mocked. Then the news reached a man hundreds of miles away — Nehemiah, a cupbearer in a foreign palace, a man with a good position and no obligation to care. But when he heard, his heart broke. "So it was, when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned for many days; I was fasting and praying before the God of heaven" (Nehemiah 1:4). He did not rush off with a quick fix. He wept, he fasted, he prayed — and only then did he make a plan. That sequence is the whole of this unit in seed form. Biblical vision and strategic planning do not begin with a whiteboard and a slogan. They begin with a burden from God that breaks a man's heart, drives him to his knees, and only then moves his hands to build. In Unit 2 we saw the leader is a shepherd and steward of what is God's. Now we ask: where is he taking the flock, and how does he know?
blocks.es_reference: Los muros de Jerusalén yacían en ruinas. Las puertas estaban quemadas, el pueblo desanimado, y los enemigos en derredor se burlaban. Entonces la noticia llegó a un hombre a cientos de kilómetros — Nehemías, un copero en un palacio extranjero, un hombre con buena posición y sin obligación de preocuparse. Pero cuando oyó, se le rompió el corazón. "Y cuando oí estas palabras, me senté y lloré, e hice duelo por algunos días; y ayuné y oré delante del Dios de los cielos" (Nehemías 1:4). No salió corriendo con una solución rápida. Lloró, ayunó, oró — y solo entonces hizo un plan. Esa secuencia es toda esta unidad en semilla. La visión bíblica y la planificación estratégica no comienzan con un pizarrón y un lema. Comienzan con una carga de Dios que rompe el corazón de un hombre, lo lleva de rodillas, y solo entonces mueve sus manos a edificar. En la Unidad 2 vimos que el líder es pastor y mayordomo de lo que es de Dios. Ahora preguntamos: ¿a dónde lleva al rebaño, y cómo lo sabe?

blocks.en: "When I heard these words, I sat down and wept... I was fasting and praying before the God of heaven." — Nehemiah 1:4 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Y cuando oí estas palabras, me senté y lloré... y ayuné y oré delante del Dios de los cielos." — Nehemías 1:4 (RVG)

blocks.en: Vision Is Not a Slogan
blocks.es_reference: La visión no es un lema

blocks.en: The word vision has been so worn down by the business world that we must rescue it before we can use it. In the mouth of a marketing department, a vision is a clever sentence on a wall. In the mouth of Scripture, it is something far weightier. "Where there is no vision, the people perish" (Proverbs 29:18). The older sense of that word is revelation — a word from God — and the proverb pairs it with keeping the law, so that true vision is never a leader's private ambition dressed up in spiritual language. It is a God-given burden that aligns with God's Word and leads to action. A vision that contradicts Scripture is not vision but presumption. A vision that never moves beyond a framed sentence is not vision but decoration. Real vision is a clear, Spirit-given sense of what God would have this people become and do — and it carries within it the energy to actually pursue it. Without it, the proverb warns, the people scatter and perish; they cast off restraint and drift, because no one has told them where they are going or why.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra visión ha sido tan gastada por el mundo de los negocios que debemos rescatarla antes de poder usarla. En boca de un departamento de mercadeo, una visión es una frase ingeniosa en la pared. En boca de la Escritura, es algo mucho más pesado. "Sin visión, el pueblo perece" (Proverbios 29:18). El sentido antiguo de esa palabra es revelación — una palabra de Dios — y el proverbio la une con guardar la ley, de modo que la verdadera visión nunca es la ambición privada de un líder disfrazada de lenguaje espiritual. Es una carga dada por Dios que concuerda con la Palabra de Dios y conduce a la acción. Una visión que contradice la Escritura no es visión sino presunción. Una visión que nunca pasa de una frase enmarcada no es visión sino decoración. La verdadera visión es un sentido claro, dado por el Espíritu, de lo que Dios quiere que este pueblo llegue a ser y a hacer — y lleva en sí misma la energía para de veras perseguirlo. Sin ella, advierte el proverbio, el pueblo se dispersa y perece; se desenfrena y deriva, porque nadie le ha dicho a dónde va ni por qué.

blocks.en: It Begins on the Knees
blocks.es_reference: Comienza de rodillas

blocks.en: Mark the order in Nehemiah, because we are forever tempted to reverse it. Before he surveyed a single stone, before he requested a single resource, before he spoke a single word of his plan to anyone, Nehemiah prayed for days. His vision was born in the presence of God, not in a strategy session. And this is the first safeguard against the counterfeit: a vision that is truly from God will have been bathed in prayer, while a vision that is merely a leader's good idea will usually have skipped straight to the planning. The praying is not a delay before the real work; it is the root from which real work grows. The leader who prays first receives a burden he can trust, because he has tested it before God and not merely admired it in his own mind. Brother, if you want to lead God's people somewhere, begin where Nehemiah began — on your knees, fasting and praying before the God of heaven, until the burden He gives you is unmistakably His and not merely yours.
blocks.es_reference: Note el orden en Nehemías, porque siempre estamos tentados a invertirlo. Antes de inspeccionar una sola piedra, antes de pedir un solo recurso, antes de hablar una sola palabra de su plan a nadie, Nehemías oró por días. Su visión nació en la presencia de Dios, no en una sesión de estrategia. Y esta es la primera salvaguarda contra lo falso: una visión que de veras viene de Dios habrá sido bañada en oración, mientras que una visión que es solo la buena idea de un líder por lo general habrá saltado directamente a la planificación. El orar no es una demora antes de la obra verdadera; es la raíz de la cual crece la obra verdadera. El líder que ora primero recibe una carga en la que puede confiar, porque la ha probado delante de Dios y no solo admirado en su propia mente. Hermano, si quiere llevar al pueblo de Dios a algún lugar, comience donde comenzó Nehemías — de rodillas, ayunando y orando delante del Dios de los cielos, hasta que la carga que Él le dé sea inconfundiblemente suya y no solo de usted.

blocks.en: From Burden to Plan
blocks.es_reference: De la carga al plan

blocks.en: But notice what Nehemiah does after he prays: he plans, and he plans carefully. He does not float into Jerusalem on a cloud of good intentions. He arrives, and for three nights he rides out quietly to survey the broken walls with his own eyes before he says a word (Nehemiah 2:11-16). When he finally stands before the king, he has an answer ready for every question — how long the work will take, what letters he will need for safe passage, what timber he will require from the king's forest (Nehemiah 2:6-8). This is the divine and the human joined again: the burden came from God on his knees, but the plan came from God through his diligence. Prayer did not replace planning; it grounded it. The leader who only prays and never plans presumes upon God; the leader who only plans and never prays presumes upon himself. Nehemiah did both, in that order, and that is biblical strategic planning — a God-given burden worked out through careful, counted, concrete steps.
blocks.es_reference: Pero note lo que Nehemías hace después de orar: planea, y planea con cuidado. No flota hacia Jerusalén en una nube de buenas intenciones. Llega, y por tres noches sale en silencio a inspeccionar los muros rotos con sus propios ojos antes de decir una palabra (Nehemías 2:11-16). Cuando por fin está ante el rey, tiene lista una respuesta para cada pregunta — cuánto durará la obra, qué cartas necesitará para pasar seguro, qué madera requerirá del bosque del rey (Nehemías 2:6-8). Esto es lo divino y lo humano unidos otra vez: la carga vino de Dios sobre sus rodillas, pero el plan vino de Dios mediante su diligencia. La oración no reemplazó la planificación; la fundamentó. El líder que solo ora y nunca planea presume de Dios; el líder que solo planea y nunca ora presume de sí mismo. Nehemías hizo ambas cosas, en ese orden, y eso es la planificación estratégica bíblica — una carga dada por Dios desarrollada mediante pasos cuidadosos, contados y concretos.

blocks.en: Lest anyone think such careful counting is somehow beneath faith, hear that the Lord Jesus Himself commended it. "For which of you, intending to build a tower, does not sit down first and count the cost, whether he has enough to finish it?" (Luke 14:28). Christ took it for granted that a wise builder counts before he begins, and He warned that the man who lays a foundation he cannot finish becomes a mockery to all who watch. Counting the cost is not unbelief; it is obedience to plain wisdom, and we will return to it when we take up budgeting in a later unit. For now, fix the principle: the leader who has received a burden from God must also, like Nehemiah and like the wise tower-builder, sit down and reckon honestly what it will take to finish, so that the vision is not abandoned half-built for lack of forethought.
blocks.es_reference: Y para que nadie piense que tal cuidado al contar es de algún modo indigno de la fe, oiga que el Señor Jesús mismo lo encomió. "Porque ¿quién de vosotros, queriendo edificar una torre, no se sienta primero y cuenta el costo, para ver si tiene lo que necesita para acabarla?" (Lucas 14:28). Cristo dio por sentado que el constructor sabio cuenta antes de comenzar, y advirtió que el hombre que pone un cimiento que no puede terminar se vuelve burla de todos los que lo ven. Contar el costo no es incredulidad; es obediencia a la sabiduría sencilla, y volveremos a ello cuando tratemos el presupuesto en una unidad posterior. Por ahora, fije el principio: el líder que ha recibido una carga de Dios debe también, como Nehemías y como el sabio constructor de la torre, sentarse y calcular con honradez lo que costará terminar, para que la visión no se abandone a medio edificar por falta de previsión.

blocks.en: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, does not sit down first and count the cost?" — Luke 14:28 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Porque ¿quién de vosotros, queriendo edificar una torre, no se sienta primero y cuenta el costo?" — Lucas 14:28 (RVG)

blocks.en: Let me tell you a story. It never happened to one church exactly — but I have watched its shape in many. Two churches sat in the same town. The first had no vision at all; it simply opened its doors each Sunday out of habit, did this year what it did last year, and slowly grew older and smaller, never quite able to say why it existed or where it was going. The people did not rebel; they simply drifted away, one at a time, because nothing called them anywhere. The second church had a pastor who had wept and prayed over his town until God laid a clear burden on him, and then he had counted the cost and made a plan, and he stood up one Sunday and said, in effect, "Here is where God is calling us, and here is how we will go." The people caught fire. They gave, they served, they built. Same town, same gospel. But one church perished for lack of vision, and the other rose up to build, exactly as the proverb said.
blocks.es_reference: Déjeme contarle una historia. No le sucedió a una sola iglesia exactamente — pero he visto su forma en muchas. Dos iglesias estaban en el mismo pueblo. La primera no tenía visión alguna; simplemente abría sus puertas cada domingo por costumbre, hacía este año lo que hizo el anterior, y lentamente envejecía y menguaba, sin poder nunca decir bien por qué existía ni a dónde iba. La gente no se rebeló; sencillamente se fue alejando, uno a uno, porque nada la llamaba a ninguna parte. La segunda iglesia tenía un pastor que había llorado y orado por su pueblo hasta que Dios puso sobre él una carga clara, y luego había contado el costo y hecho un plan, y se levantó un domingo y dijo, en efecto: "Aquí es a donde Dios nos llama, y así iremos". La gente se encendió. Dieron, sirvieron, edificaron. Mismo pueblo, mismo evangelio. Pero una iglesia pereció por falta de visión, y la otra se levantó a edificar, tal como dijo el proverbio.

blocks.en: Expect Opposition
blocks.es_reference: Espere oposición

blocks.en: Here is a truth no honest course on vision can omit: the moment you set out to build something for God, opposition will come. Nehemiah had barely begun before Sanballat and Tobiah were mocking, scheming, and threatening (Nehemiah 4). This did not mean the vision was wrong; it meant the vision was real. A leader who expects every God-given plan to glide forward on universal applause will be paralyzed by the first opposition and conclude he must have missed God's will. Nehemiah teaches the opposite. He answered the mockers with a settled confidence: "The God of heaven Himself will prosper us; therefore we His servants will arise and build" (Nehemiah 2:20). And when the threats grew serious, he did the two things faith always does together — "we made our prayer to our God, and... set a watch against them day and night" (Nehemiah 4:9). They prayed, and they posted a guard. The men built with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other. Vision does not remove opposition; it gives a leader the resolve to keep building through it, trusting God and taking sensible precautions at the same time.
blocks.es_reference: He aquí una verdad que ningún curso honesto sobre la visión puede omitir: en el momento en que se proponga edificar algo para Dios, vendrá la oposición. Apenas había comenzado Nehemías cuando Sanbalat y Tobías ya se burlaban, conspiraban y amenazaban (Nehemías 4). Esto no significaba que la visión fuera errónea; significaba que la visión era real. El líder que espera que todo plan dado por Dios avance sobre un aplauso unánime quedará paralizado ante la primera oposición y concluirá que erró la voluntad de Dios. Nehemías enseña lo contrario. Respondió a los burladores con una confianza firme: "El Dios de los cielos, él nos prosperará, y nosotros sus siervos nos levantaremos y edificaremos" (Nehemías 2:20). Y cuando las amenazas se hicieron serias, hizo las dos cosas que la fe siempre hace juntas — "oramos a nuestro Dios, y... pusimos guarda contra ellos de día y de noche" (Nehemías 4:9). Oraron, y pusieron guardia. Los hombres edificaban con una herramienta en una mano y un arma en la otra. La visión no quita la oposición; le da al líder la resolución de seguir edificando a través de ella, confiando en Dios y tomando precauciones sensatas a la vez.

blocks.en: "The God of heaven Himself will prosper us; therefore we His servants will arise and build." — Nehemiah 2:20 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "El Dios de los cielos, él nos prosperará, y nosotros sus siervos nos levantaremos y edificaremos." — Nehemías 2:20 (RVG)

blocks.en: Vision Must Be Shared and Owned
blocks.es_reference: La visión debe compartirse y hacerse propia

blocks.en: One last thing, and it is the difference between a vision and a daydream. A vision locked in the leader's head accomplishes nothing; it must be shared until the people own it as their own. Watch how Nehemiah does it. He does not announce his plan and command obedience. He tells the people how the hand of God had been on him, lays out the need plainly, and then says, "Come, and let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer be a reproach" (Nehemiah 2:17). And the response is the goal of all vision-casting: "So they said, 'Let us rise up and build.' Then they set their hands to this good work" (Nehemiah 2:18). Notice the shift. The vision that began as Nehemiah's burden became the people's own resolve — "let us rise up." A vision the people merely hear will die; a vision the people own will build a wall in fifty-two days. So the leader's task is not only to receive the vision on his knees and shape it into a plan, but to carry it to the people in such a way that it becomes theirs — rooted in God's Word, aimed at God's glory, and owned by God's people, who then rise up together to build.
blocks.es_reference: Una última cosa, y es la diferencia entre una visión y un sueño despierto. Una visión encerrada en la cabeza del líder no logra nada; debe compartirse hasta que el pueblo la haga suya. Vea cómo lo hace Nehemías. No anuncia su plan y exige obediencia. Le cuenta al pueblo cómo la mano de Dios había estado sobre él, expone la necesidad con claridad, y luego dice: "Venid, y edifiquemos el muro de Jerusalén, y no estemos más en oprobio" (Nehemías 2:17). Y la respuesta es la meta de toda comunicación de visión: "Y dijeron: Levantémonos y edifiquemos. Así esforzaron sus manos para bien" (Nehemías 2:18). Note el cambio. La visión que comenzó como la carga de Nehemías se convirtió en la resolución propia del pueblo — "levantémonos". Una visión que el pueblo solo oye morirá; una visión que el pueblo hace suya edificará un muro en cincuenta y dos días. Así que la tarea del líder no es solo recibir la visión de rodillas y darle forma de plan, sino llevarla al pueblo de tal modo que se vuelva suya — arraigada en la Palabra de Dios, dirigida a la gloria de Dios, y hecha propia por el pueblo de Dios, que entonces se levanta unido a edificar.

blocks.en: "So they said, 'Let us rise up and build.' Then they set their hands to this good work." — Nehemiah 2:18 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Y dijeron: Levantémonos y edifiquemos. Así esforzaron sus manos para bien." — Nehemías 2:18 (RVG)

sa.prompt: Explain the biblical meaning of 'vision' and why Proverbs 29:18 matters for a church.
sa.model: In its biblical sense, vision is not a marketing slogan but a God-given burden, a kind of revelation, that aligns with God's Word and leads to action. Proverbs 29:18 warns that where there is no vision the people perish, casting off restraint and drifting because no one has told them where they are going. The proverb pairs vision with keeping the law, so true vision is never private ambition dressed in spiritual language; it must agree with Scripture. For a church it matters because without a clear, God-given direction the people scatter, while a true vision gives them direction and the energy to pursue God's purpose together.

sa.prompt: Why does the unit insist that vision must begin in prayer, and how does Nehemiah model this?
sa.model: The unit insists vision must begin in prayer because a vision truly from God is born and tested in His presence, while a vision that is merely a leader's good idea usually skips straight to planning. Nehemiah models this: before he surveyed a stone, requested a resource, or spoke his plan, he wept, fasted, and prayed for days before the God of heaven. The praying was not a delay before the real work but the root from which it grew. By praying first, the leader receives a burden he can trust, having tested it before God rather than merely admiring it in his own mind.

sa.prompt: How does Nehemiah hold prayer and planning together, and what error lies on each side?
sa.model: Nehemiah holds prayer and planning together by doing both, in order: the burden came from God on his knees, but the plan came from God through his diligence. After praying he surveyed the broken walls himself by night and had a careful, counted answer ready for the king about time, letters, and timber. Prayer did not replace planning; it grounded it. The error on each side is clear: the leader who only prays and never plans presumes upon God, expecting results without diligence, while the leader who only plans and never prays presumes upon himself, trusting his own competence instead of God.

sa.prompt: Why should a leader EXPECT opposition, and how did Nehemiah respond to it?
sa.model: A leader should expect opposition because the moment he sets out to build something for God, opposition comes; Sanballat and Tobiah mocked and threatened almost as soon as Nehemiah began. Opposition does not mean the vision is wrong but that it is real, and a leader who expects universal applause will be paralyzed by the first resistance. Nehemiah responded with settled confidence that the God of heaven would prosper His servants, and he did the two things faith always does together: they made their prayer to God and set a watch day and night. He trusted God and took sensible precautions, building with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other.

sa.prompt: Why must a vision be shared and owned, and how did Nehemiah accomplish this?
sa.model: A vision must be shared and owned because a vision locked in the leader's head is only a daydream that accomplishes nothing; it builds nothing until the people make it their own. Nehemiah accomplished this not by commanding obedience but by telling the people how God's hand had been on him, naming the need plainly, and inviting them: 'let us build the wall.' The people responded, 'Let us rise up and build,' and set their hands to the work. The vision that began as Nehemiah's burden had become the people's own resolve, and an owned vision built the wall in fifty-two days, while a vision the people merely hear would have died.

sa.prompt: What is the danger of a church with no vision, as pictured in the illustration?
sa.model: The danger of a church with no vision is that it drifts and slowly declines. In the illustration the first church simply opened its doors out of habit, doing this year what it did last year, unable to say why it existed or where it was going. The people did not rebel; they drifted away one at a time because nothing called them anywhere. This is exactly what Proverbs 29:18 warns: without vision the people perish, scattering for lack of direction and purpose. A church may keep the same gospel and the same building yet quietly die for want of a clear, God-given sense of where He is calling it to go.

sa.prompt: How does the divine/human pattern appear in Nehemiah's vision and planning?
sa.model: The divine/human pattern appears in that Nehemiah's vision and planning joined God's work and man's effort. The burden came from God as Nehemiah wept and prayed; it was divine in origin, not something he manufactured. But the plan came from God through Nehemiah's own diligence as he surveyed the walls and counted what the work would require. Prayer grounded the planning rather than replacing it. This is the same pattern that runs through Scripture: God accomplishes His purpose through human means, so the leader both seeks God on his knees for the burden and works diligently with his hands and mind to carry it out.

sa.prompt: What safeguards keep a 'vision' from being merely a leader's private ambition?
sa.model: Two safeguards keep a vision from being merely private ambition. First, it must align with God's Word: Proverbs 29:18 pairs vision with keeping the law, and a vision that contradicts Scripture is presumption, not vision. Second, it must be born and tested in prayer, as Nehemiah's was, so the leader has weighed it before God rather than merely admiring his own good idea. A vision that has been bathed in prayer and measured against Scripture, and that aims at God's glory rather than the leader's name, can be trusted as God-given; one that skips prayer, ignores the Word, or serves the leader's ambition cannot.

sa.prompt: Describe Nehemiah's full sequence from hearing the news to the people building.
sa.model: Nehemiah's sequence runs from burden to building in clear steps. First he heard the news and was broken by it, weeping, fasting, and praying for days before the God of heaven. Then he planned carefully, surveying the broken walls by night and preparing concrete requests of the king. Then he shared the vision with the people, telling how God's hand was on him and inviting them to build, until they made it their own and said, 'Let us rise up and build.' As they worked, opposition came from Sanballat and Tobiah, and Nehemiah met it by praying and setting a watch. The result was a wall finished in fifty-two days, the fruit of a God-given burden carried through prayer, planning, shared ownership, and perseverance.

sa.prompt: Summarize Unit 3: how does biblical strategic planning move from burden to a finished work?
sa.model: Unit 3 teaches that biblical strategic planning moves from burden to finished work along Nehemiah's path. It begins not with a slogan but with a God-given burden that breaks the leader's heart and drives him to prayer, where the vision is born and tested before God and measured against His Word. From prayer it moves to careful planning, the burden worked out through diligent, counted, concrete steps. Then the vision is shared with the people until they own it and say, 'Let us rise up and build.' Opposition is expected and met with both prayer and sensible precaution. So a God-given vision, rooted in His Word and aimed at His glory, becomes a plan, becomes the people's own resolve, and finally becomes a finished work for God.
